# Reliability Statistics for Robot Manipulation: Reporting Success Rates, Confidence Intervals, and Mean Cycles Between Interventions

## 1. The Problem: How the Field Currently Reports Success

The dominant metric in physical robot-manipulation evaluation is "success rate"—the percentage of autonomous runs that succeed. Kress-Gazit et al. (2024, preprint) argue that this practice is insufficient: "it is common for papers to report this number with little to no information regarding the number of runs, the initial conditions, and the success criteria, little to no narrative description of the behaviors and failures observed, and little to no statistical analysis of the findings" (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3). A recent audit of the five most-cited manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0) found that the majority of reported performance gaps between policies are statistically inconclusive when examined with paired Wald tests: across LIBERO, only 20.8% of 789 comparisons were provably significant at the 5% level (jiang2026whatarewe pages 5-7).

The following table summarizes how major benchmarks actually report results, their trial counts, and whether they include any form of uncertainty estimate.

| Paper / benchmark | Year | Venue | Robot arm | Trials per task / condition | Success criterion | Statistical method | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| YCB Benchmarking | 2015 | IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine | Various platforms | Typically 10 | Task-specific completion, such as successful peg insertion | Raw successes/trials; no proportion CI | Also reports timed-run means and SDs for some protocols; DOI: [10.1109/MRA.2015.2448951](https://doi.org/10.1109/MRA.2015.2448951) (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35) |
| NIST Assembly Task Board | 2020 | IEEE RA-L | Platform-independent | User-selected number | Autonomous completion of an assembly or disassembly task/subtask; manual or teleoperated intervention prohibited | Binomial-CDF reliability bound using successes, trials, and confidence level; completion-time mean, SD, and 95% CI | Protocol variant and randomization level must remain fixed across systems; DOI: [10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869](https://doi.org/10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869) (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9) |

*Table: Comparison of trial counts, success definitions, and uncertainty-reporting practices in major physical robot-manipulation studies. It highlights the historically common use of small raw success fractions and the more recent adoption of Wilson or other finite-sample confidence intervals.*

## 2. Binomial Confidence Intervals for Binary Task Success

### 2.1 Framing the Problem

Each manipulation trial is naturally modeled as a Bernoulli random variable X ∈ {0,1} with unknown success probability p (hietanen2021benchmarkingposeestimation pages 5-8). The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol defines reliability as "the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task," computed from "a confidence level (CL), the number of successes (m), and the number of independent trials (n)" using the binomial cumulative distribution function (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9). This requires independent, identically distributed trials—a condition that Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L) emphasize must be ensured by a pre-specified testing plan, warning that practices such as "running policy rollouts until enough favorable outcomes are observed" violate the i.i.d. assumption (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4).

### 2.2 Clopper–Pearson (Exact) Intervals

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 3-4, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 1-3). The two-sided 100(1−α)% interval allocates α/2 to each tail. Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 8-11). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5).

### 2.3 Wilson Score Intervals

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (zhang2511experiencesfrombenchmarking pages 4-5); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 8-11).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 9-13).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6).

The following table provides the exact trial counts for several practically relevant reliability targets.

| Desired lower bound on success probability | Confidence level | Bound type | Required trials—all must succeed | Derivation / formula |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **59** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil58.40\rceil=59\) (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 95% | Two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson | **72** | Equal tails use \(\alpha/2=0.025\): \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.025)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil71.92\rceil=72\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | Approximately 95% | Rule-of-three approximation | **≈60** | \(n\approx3/(1-0.95)=60\); use the exact one-sided result, 59, for a formal claim (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6) |
| \(p \ge 0.90\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **29** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.90)\right\rceil=\lceil28.43\rceil=29\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5) |
| \(p \ge 0.99\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **299** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.99)\right\rceil=\lceil298.07\rceil=299\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 99% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **90** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.01)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil89.78\rceil=90\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5) |
| \(p \ge 0.80\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **14** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.80)\right\rceil=\lceil13.43\rceil=14\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5) |


*Table: Minimum all-success trial counts needed for selected lower-bound reliability claims. The distinction between a one-sided certification bound and a two-sided confidence interval materially changes the required sample size.*

**Critical implication for low-cost arms:** Most published manipulation papers use far fewer trials than the 59 required for a one-sided 95%/95% claim. ALOHA uses 25 real-robot trials per task (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 8-10); Mobile ALOHA uses 20 (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8); FurnitureBench uses 10 (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 6-7, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10); YCB protocols use 10 (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulation pages 34-35, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35); and ArmnetBench uses 30 (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7). With 25 all-success trials, the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound on p is only 0.05^(1/25) ≈ 0.887, not 0.95. To genuinely certify 95% success at 95% confidence, 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are necessary.

## 4. Mean Cycles Between Interventions and MTBF

### 4.1 In Lab Automation

Laboratory automation systems report reliability using mean time between failures (MTBF) measured in calendar days or operating hours. Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection, peer-reviewed) report that BD Kiestra TLA and WCA automated bacteriology systems achieve approximately 100 days MTBF, while the Copan WASPLab achieves approximately 95 days, with the caveat that "MTBF is difficult to specify because it depends substantially on system configuration, overall system complexity, the number and variety of samples processed each day, and user-induced factors" (croxatto2016laboratoryautomationin pages 11-13). In industrial manufacturing with Digital Twin/IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, Mostofa (2024) reports baseline MTBF of 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI [1,431.5, 1,541.1]) across 220 assets including robotic systems, improving to 2,176.8 hours post-intervention (mostofa2024digitaltwinand pages 26-27, mostofa2024digitaltwinand pages 27-29).

### 4.2 In Field Robotics

Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology, peer-reviewed) note that "the Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) for robots in field environments is often within a few hours" (honig2018understandingandresolving pages 3-5), highlighting the substantial gap between industrial automation and research robot reliability.

### 4.3 Explicit Gap: No Standard for Mean Cycles Between Interventions in Manipulation

**No published standard exists for reporting "mean cycles between interventions" (MCBI) as a reliability metric for robot manipulation tasks.** The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol uses binomial success probability and completion time (mean, SD, and 95% CI), but does not define a cycles-between-interventions metric (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9). Lab automation papers report MTBF in time units rather than task cycles (croxatto2016laboratoryautomationin pages 11-13). For teams running repeated pick-and-place or assembly cycles on low-cost arms, defining and reporting MCBI—the mean number of autonomous task cycles completed before a human must intervene to reset, fix a jam, or correct an error—would fill a genuine gap in the literature. This metric can be modeled as a geometric or negative-binomial random variable and reported with appropriate confidence intervals.

## 5. Best Practices for Reporting: A Synthesis

Based on the surveyed literature, the following reporting practices are recommended for teams benchmarking low-cost arms:

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3, zhang2511experiencesfrombenchmarking pages 4-5), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 3-4). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 3-5).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 9-13). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (jiang2026whatarewe pages 5-7).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 10-11).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

## 7. Publication Status of Cited Sources

The following papers cited in this review are **preprints** (not yet peer-reviewed in a journal or major conference proceedings): Kress-Gazit et al. (2024), Jiang et al. (2026), Selvaraj et al. (2026, ArmnetBench), Wu et al. (2024, RoboMIND), Zhao et al. (2023, ALOHA), Fu et al. (2024, Mobile ALOHA), Zhang et al. (2025, Experiences Benchmarking VLA), Fan et al. (2026, SafeVLA-Bench), Zha et al. (2026, LAP), Petkov et al. (2026, LADDER), and Chen et al. (2026, RoboDojo). The following are **peer-reviewed**: Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L), Kimble et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Calli et al. (2015, IEEE Robotics & Automation Magazine), Vagas et al. (2026, IEEE RA-L), Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics), Heo et al. (2025, IJRR), Luo et al. (2024, IJRR), Denoun et al. (2023, IEEE Transactions on Robotics), Morgan et al. (2020, IEEE RA-L), Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection), Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology), Cadène et al. (2026, ICLR), and Budde et al. (2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science).

# Reliability Statistics for Robot Manipulation: Reporting Success Rates, Confidence Intervals, and Mean Cycles Between Interventions

## 1. The Problem: How the Field Currently Reports Success

The dominant metric in physical robot-manipulation evaluation is "success rate"—the percentage of autonomous runs that succeed. Kress-Gazit et al. (2024, preprint) argue that this practice is insufficient: "it is common for papers to report this number with little to no information regarding the number of runs, the initial conditions, and the success criteria, little to no narrative description of the behaviors and failures observed, and little to no statistical analysis of the findings" (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012). A recent audit of the five most-cited manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0) found that the majority of reported performance gaps between policies are statistically inconclusive when examined with paired Wald tests: across LIBERO, only 20.8% of 789 comparisons were provably significant at the 5% level (pqac-00000042).

## 2. Binomial Confidence Intervals for Binary Task Success

### 2.1 Framing the Problem

Each manipulation trial is naturally modeled as a Bernoulli random variable X ∈ {0,1} with unknown success probability p (pqac-00000007). The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol defines reliability as "the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task," computed from "a confidence level (CL), the number of successes (m), and the number of independent trials (n)" using the binomial cumulative distribution function (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000037). This requires independent, identically distributed trials—a condition that Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L) emphasize must be ensured by a pre-specified testing plan, warning that practices such as "running policy rollouts until enough favorable outcomes are observed" violate the i.i.d. assumption (pqac-00000040).

### 2.2 Clopper–Pearson (Exact) Intervals

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055). The two-sided 100(1−α)% interval allocates α/2 to each tail. Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (pqac-00000056). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000051).

### 2.3 Wilson Score Intervals

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (pqac-00000016). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (pqac-00000016). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (pqac-00000023); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (pqac-00000056).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000010).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053).

The following table provides the exact trial counts for several practically relevant reliability targets.

| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 95% | Two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson | **72** | Equal tails use \(\alpha/2=0.025\): \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.025)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil71.92\rceil=72\) (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000053) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | Approximately 95% | Rule-of-three approximation | **≈60** | \(n\approx3/(1-0.95)=60\); use the exact one-sided result, 59, for a formal claim (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052) |
| \(p \ge 0.90\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **29** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.90)\right\rceil=\lceil28.43\rceil=29\) (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051) |
| \(p \ge 0.99\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **299** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.99)\right\rceil=\lceil298.07\rceil=299\) (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 99% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **90** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.01)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil89.78\rceil=90\) (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051) |

**Critical implication for low-cost arms:** Most published manipulation papers use far fewer trials than the 59 required for a one-sided 95%/95% claim. ALOHA uses 25 real-robot trials per task (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000028); Mobile ALOHA uses 20 (pqac-00000024); FurnitureBench uses 10 (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062); YCB protocols use 10 (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015); and ArmnetBench uses 30 (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059). With 25 all-success trials, the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound on p is only 0.05^(1/25) ≈ 0.887, not 0.95. To genuinely certify 95% success at 95% confidence, 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are necessary.

## 4. Mean Cycles Between Interventions and MTBF

### 4.1 In Lab Automation

Laboratory automation systems report reliability using mean time between failures (MTBF) measured in calendar days or operating hours. Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection, peer-reviewed) report that BD Kiestra TLA and WCA automated bacteriology systems achieve approximately 100 days MTBF, while the Copan WASPLab achieves approximately 95 days, with the caveat that "MTBF is difficult to specify because it depends substantially on system configuration, overall system complexity, the number and variety of samples processed each day, and user-induced factors" (pqac-00000030). In industrial manufacturing with Digital Twin/IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, Mostofa (2024) reports baseline MTBF of 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI [1,431.5, 1,541.1]) across 220 assets including robotic systems, improving to 2,176.8 hours post-intervention (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033).

### 4.2 In Field Robotics

Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology, peer-reviewed) note that "the Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) for robots in field environments is often within a few hours" (pqac-00000049), highlighting the substantial gap between industrial automation and research robot reliability.

### 4.3 Explicit Gap: No Standard for Mean Cycles Between Interventions in Manipulation

**No published standard exists for reporting "mean cycles between interventions" (MCBI) as a reliability metric for robot manipulation tasks.** The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol uses binomial success probability and completion time (mean, SD, and 95% CI), but does not define a cycles-between-interventions metric (pqac-00000037). Lab automation papers report MTBF in time units rather than task cycles (pqac-00000030). For teams running repeated pick-and-place or assembly cycles on low-cost arms, defining and reporting MCBI—the mean number of autonomous task cycles completed before a human must intervene to reset, fix a jam, or correct an error—would fill a genuine gap in the literature. This metric can be modeled as a geometric or negative-binomial random variable and reported with appropriate confidence intervals.

## 5. Best Practices for Reporting: A Synthesis

Based on the surveyed literature, the following reporting practices are recommended for teams benchmarking low-cost arms:

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (pqac-00000003).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (pqac-00000016). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (pqac-00000062). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (pqac-00000058).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (pqac-00000013).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000012).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (pqac-00000037).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (pqac-00000040).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000058) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000010). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (pqac-00000042).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000060).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (pqac-00000046).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (pqac-00000015).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (pqac-00000037).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000059).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

## 7. Publication Status of Cited Sources

The following papers cited in this review are **preprints** (not yet peer-reviewed in a journal or major conference proceedings): Kress-Gazit et al. (2024), Jiang et al. (2026), Selvaraj et al. (2026, SafeVLA-Bench), Zha et al. (2026, LAP), Petkov et al. (2026, LADDER), and Chen et al. (2026, RoboDojo). The following are **peer-reviewed**: Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L), Kimble et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection), Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology), Cadène et al. (2026, ICLR), and Budde et al. (2025, Lecture Notes in Computer Science).

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends reporting robot-manipulation success as a statistically justified lower confidence bound on the unknown probability of task success, rather than reporting only the observed success percentage. Confidence and tightness should be stated explicitly: confidence describes how often the bound covers the true success probability, while tightness describes how close the bound tends to be to that probability. For binary success/failure outcomes, the paper revisits the Clopper–Pearson approach and presents a tighter binomial bound that can achieve a user-specified confidence level while minimizing rollouts. The method is distribution-free and does not depend on robot state dimensionality, observation dimensionality, policy structure, hardware, or environment physics, but it assumes independent and identically distributed performance measurements. The excerpt also emphasizes the trade-off among confidence, tightness, and sample size. It does not provide the numerical trial count for claiming 95% success with 95% confidence, nor does it discuss Wilson intervals specifically. That number therefore requires selecting a convention—such as a one-sided versus two-sided interval—and calculating the relevant binomial lower bound, typically assuming all observed trials succeed.

Statistical analysis should accompany the observed success rate, using interval estimates or bounds under a frequentist approach, or posterior parameter estimates under a Bayesian approach. contexts.context: The excerpt models robot-task outcomes as Bernoulli trials: each manipulation attempt is either successful (X = 1) or unsuccessful (X = 0), with success probability p. For homogeneous trials, the maximum-likelihood estimate of the success rate is the observed sample average, i.e., the number of successes divided by the number of trials. The paper cautions that pose-dependent manipulation trials are generally non-homogeneous because success probability varies with the object pose and depends on factors such as object shape, gripper properties, and task requirements. Consequently, a simple pooled binomial estimate is only directly justified when trials share a common success probability, or when an appropriate model accounts for variation. This excerpt does not specify Wilson, Clopper–Pearson, or other confidence-interval procedures, nor does it provide a minimum trial count for claiming a 95% success rate with 95% confidence. Determining that count requires an explicit statistical convention—particularly whether the claim means an exact observed rate of 95%, a lower confidence bound of at least 95%, or a one-sided binomial guarantee—and assumptions about independent, identically distributed trials.

Success-rate reporting should therefore identify the number of successful outcomes (m), the total number of independent trials (n), and the confidence level (CL), using the binomial cumulative distribution function to establish a confidence-based bound on the success probability. For a claim of at least 95% success with 95% confidence when every trial succeeds, the standard one-sided exact binomial calculation requires 59 independent trials: 0.95^n ≤ 0.05. If a two-sided 95% interval is required, the corresponding exact lower-bound calculation is more conservative and requires 73 all-success trials. These trial counts assume zero observed failures and should be stated explicitly, along with the interval method and whether the confidence bound is one- or two-sided. contexts.context: The excerpt provides a statistical framework for reporting success rates in pass-fail robotic manipulation tests, but it does not discuss ALOHA, LeRobot, Franka, or UR5e evaluations specifically, nor does it give typical trial counts for those platforms. For tests with no observed failures, the required number of trials n is determined from the desired confidence level CL and probability of success PS using n = ln(1−CL)/ln(PS). The text identifies 0.95 as a typical confidence level and notes that this calculation assumes no failures occur in the n trials. When failures are observed, success probability should instead be estimated from the number of successes m and independent trials n using a binomial cumulative distribution inequality; PS is selected as the minimum value satisfying the specified confidence requirement. Thus, papers can report a success rate as successes divided by trials, together with the trial count and, ideally, a confidence-based bound or interval derived from the binomial distribution. The excerpt does not establish whether commonly reported robot manipulation results include confidence intervals, so platform-specific papers must be checked individually. It also distinguishes pass-fail sample sizing from continuous measurements, where preliminary trials (for example, ten trials) can estimate variability before determining additional samples.
contexts.question: How do papers report success rates in robot manipulation with specific numbers of trials? What are typical trial counts used in ALOHA, LeRobot, Franka, UR5e evaluations? Do they report confidence intervals?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a concrete example of reporting robot-manipulation success rates, but it does not compare trial counts across ALOHA, LeRobot, Franka, or UR5e evaluations. In this paper, every task is evaluated over 20 independent trials, with randomized object placement within workspace bounds. Trials end when the task succeeds, times out, or triggers a safety abort, such as a collision, joint-limit violation, or unsafe motion. For zero-shot experiments, results are reported as binary task success rates, together with 95% finite-sample-valid confidence intervals for the corresponding binomial proportions. Thus, a reported success percentage is based on the number of successful trials out of 20, and uncertainty is explicitly quantified. Fine-tuning experiments use staged success scores rather than only binary success, allowing partial completion to be represented—for example, reaching, grasping, and placing an object may receive intermediate scores. The supplied pages do not state typical or standard trial counts specifically for ALOHA, LeRobot, Franka, or UR5e, nor do they establish whether those benchmarks universally report confidence intervals. They only document this study’s 20-trial protocol and its use of confidence intervals for zero-shot binary success.

contexts.context: Wilson score confidence intervals are used in the excerpt to quantify uncertainty around binomial grasp-success proportions. They are recommended because they provide well-behaved coverage when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1. In the CEGB procedure, each object is tested in k canonical poses, with a repeated number of attempts per pose (denoted a). For object o and pose j, the success proportion is the number of successful attempts divided by a. Results are then summarized per object and at the dataset level using micro- and macro-average success rates. The benchmark defines a successful grasp as lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout. However, this excerpt does not provide numerical values for the actual trial count a, the number of objects or poses, or any measured success rates. It only specifies that these parameters must be reported and that the configuration may be adapted by users. Therefore, specific trial counts and success-rate results cannot be determined from pages 2–3 alone.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not define or mention Wilson score confidence intervals. It does describe how confidence intervals and repeated trials are used in cross-embodiment gripper benchmarking. In the YCB Grasp Success evaluation, each object–pose combination was tested in five attempts, and per-object success rates were calculated. The reported RGP results were a 39.5% micro-average success rate with a 95% confidence interval of [37.35, 41.55], and a 38.7% macro-average success rate with a 95% confidence interval of [22.43, 57.47]. Spherical and cylindrical objects achieved micro-average success rates above 63%. For the NIST evaluation, which measured grasp cycle time, grasp strength, and slip resistance, each experiment was repeated at least 10 times under identical conditions. Those measurements were summarized using medians and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. More generally, the benchmark protocols emphasize repeated trials, controlled conditions, and uncertainty reporting to enable comparisons across grippers. However, based on this excerpt alone, the intervals reported are identified as confidence intervals or 95% bootstrap confidence intervals, not specifically Wilson score intervals; the excerpt therefore provides no basis for explaining the Wilson method itself.

contexts.context: The excerpt states that the experiments include six real-world tasks using the ALOHA platform and that all eight evaluated tasks (including two simulated tasks) require fine-grained, bimanual manipulation. Thus, the described real-world setup uses both arms, rather than a single arm. Initial object placement is randomized: along a 15 cm reference line for real-world tasks, and within 2D regions for simulated tasks. The excerpt does not report the success-rate format, the number of trials per task, or any comparison with a Mobile ALOHA paper. contexts.context: The excerpt describes Mobile ALOHA’s success-rate reporting at both the sub-task and whole-task levels. For each sub-task, success rate is calculated as the number of successful attempts divided by the number of attempts reaching that sub-task. Because a failure causes the robot to stop, later sub-task attempts are conditioned on success in earlier subtasks; consequently, the final whole-task success rate is the product of the individual sub-task success rates. Evaluation generally uses 20 trials per task, with Cook Shrimp using only 5 trials. The paper reports whole-task results such as 95% for Wipe Wine and Call Elevator, 85% for Use Cabinet and High Five, 80% for Rinse Pan and Push Chairs, and 40% for Cook Shrimp under co-training. The system is explicitly bimanual: tasks can require both arms to grasp or coordinate simultaneously. The excerpt states that each arm has a 750 g payload limit, while coordinated use of both arms supports loads up to the combined payload; the heaviest cited pot weighs 1.4 kg. It does not specify the exact arm hardware/model or provide the corresponding reporting details for the original ALOHA paper, nor does it define an independent object-specific success criterion beyond successful completion of the relevant task/sub-task.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies mean time between failures (MTBF) as a principal quantitative reliability metric for evaluating Digital Twin- and IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, including studies involving robotic equipment. However, it does not provide a robot-specific MTBF value, a mean-cycles-between-interventions value, or a separate field-environment versus laboratory-automation comparison. Papers are described as reporting MTBF through baseline-to-post-implementation comparisons, alongside failure frequency, total failure count, failures per operating period, and mean time to failure (MTTF). MTBF is interpreted as the duration of stable operation between disruptive failures: successful predictive interventions that detect and correct degradation before breakdown are expected to increase it. The literature commonly compares conventional or baseline maintenance with predictive-maintenance implementations and reports whether MTBF increased after deployment. Reported improvements are not uniform; they vary with baseline equipment condition, maintenance maturity, operating load, machine age, fault severity, diagnostic sensitivity, and the accuracy of remaining-useful-life estimates under changing conditions. For robots or lab automation, the excerpt therefore supports using MTBF—or, if operation is naturally counted in discrete tasks, cycles between interventions—as a pre/post reliability measure, but it does not specify how many cycles, the exact averaging formula, confidence intervals, or reporting conventions for those applications.

For the full sample of 220 smart-manufacturing assets, monitored over 18,742 operating cycles and 1,284,630 cumulative machine-hours, baseline MTBF was 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI 1,431.5–1,541.1). The study also reports intervention-associated changes at the aggregate level: failure frequency fell from 1.95 to 1.18 failures per asset, while MTBF rose from 1,486.3 to 2,176.8 hours, a 46.5% increase. Thus, this paper illustrates reporting MTBF with units, dispersion, and confidence intervals, while reporting maintenance burden separately as failures and maintenance events per asset.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a numerical mean time between failures (MTBF), mean cycles between interventions, or robot-specific field/laboratory benchmark. It does, however, describe the reliability and repairable-system frameworks typically used to report or estimate such metrics. Reliability is defined as the probability that a device or system functions beyond time t, while reliability assessment covers design, testing, production, storage, and usage. For systems that undergo repairs, the generalized renewal process (GRP) is presented as a method for evaluating intervention quality and forecasting the timing of undesirable events. Its generalized renewal equation gives the expected cumulative number of recurrent events over time; this can support failure-frequency or intervention-interval estimates, although the excerpt does not identify the result explicitly as MTBF. The text notes that GRP models often require Monte Carlo simulation because closed-form solutions are generally unavailable, except for exponentially distributed event times. It also discusses imperfect repair through Kijima virtual-age models and related arithmetic reduction concepts. Overall, this source supplies methodological context for analyzing robot reliability and maintenance but does not report how papers conventionally present MTBF, cycles between interventions, operating hours, mission duration, sample size, or confidence intervals.

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on VLA benchmark significance, not physical-arm reliability. It states: “the aggregate score alone is often not enough” because gap variance requires task/sample data. For paired evaluations, it recommends a task-stratified paired Wald test using per-task, per-sample outcomes; top-line scores cannot compute it. Figure 3 (5% level) reports comparisons: LIBERO \(n=789\), CALVIN 107, SimplerEnv 122, RoboCasa 30, RoboTwin 19; provably significant shares are generally small. No Wilson/Clopper–Pearson intervals, trial-count formulas, intervention rates, or physical arm protocols appear.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe LeRobot’s evaluation of SO-100 or SO-101 robot arms, so it provides no arm-specific success rates, trial counts, task protocol, or success criterion. It does, however, outline general statistical guidance for pass-fail testing. Required sample size depends on the desired confidence level and target probability of success, using n = ln(1−CL) / ln(PS) when no failures occur across n trials. If failures are observed, the estimated minimum probability of success can instead be derived from the binomial cumulative distribution function using the number of successes m and independent trials n. The excerpt therefore supplies a general framework for reporting binary success outcomes, but not the particular protocol used by LeRobot. It also does not define what constitutes a successful manipulation or specify whether trials involve repeated grasping, pick-and-place, or another task.
contexts.question: How does LeRobot report success rates on SO-100 or SO-101 robot arms? What evaluation protocol and number of trials are used? What is the success criterion?

contexts.context: ArmnetBench v0.1 (arXiv preprint 2607.24481v1; no DOI supplied) evaluates low-cost SO-101 5-DoF arms in fixed, camera-equipped cells. Seven policies across 12 tasks produced 2,518 rollouts plus 600 demonstrations (3,118 core episodes); every episode received human three-way scoring—“successful, suboptimal, or failure”—while demonstrations were successful by construction. The protocol randomizes object positions, uses isolated containers, and releases episodes/checkpoints. It reports no Wilson or Clopper–Pearson intervals, intervention counts, mean cycles between interventions, or trial-size/power calculations. The authors explicitly state cross-cell agreement of absolute rates “remains untested.”

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the Clopper-Pearson procedure as an exact, equal-tail method for constructing a two-sided confidence interval for a binomial proportion, based on relationships among the binomial, beta, and F distributions. It does not provide the specific zero-failure sample-size calculation requested. For a demonstration with all trials successful (zero failures), the exact one-sided 95% lower confidence bound is p_L = 0.05^(1/n). Requiring p_L ≥ 0.95 gives n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.95) = 58.40, so 59 successful trials are needed. The commonly cited rule of three approximates this as 3/n ≤ 0.05, giving n = 60. If a two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson interval is required instead, use alpha/2 = 0.025: n ≥ ln(0.025)/ln(0.95) = 71.36, so 72 all-success trials are needed. Thus, the relevant distinction is whether “95% confidence” means a one-sided lower bound or a two-sided interval; the excerpt specifically discusses the two-sided Clopper-Pearson construction but does not state the numerical result.

It defines the number of successes as binomially distributed and presents a randomized uniformly most accurate lower confidence bound. contexts.context: The excerpt frames the problem as Bernoulli statistical model checking: each trial has success Xi ∈ {0,1}, the observed success proportion is the empirical mean, and a confidence interval must provide coverage at least γ. For a 95% confidence requirement, the relevant target is γ = 0.95, with soundness requiring the minimum coverage over all possible success probabilities to be at least 0.95—not merely average coverage. The excerpt does not state the Clopper–Pearson formula or the rule-of-three calculation explicitly. For the zero-failure case, the usual one-sided exact binomial/Clopper–Pearson lower confidence bound is p_L = α^(1/n), where α = 0.05. Requiring p_L ≥ 0.95 gives n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.95), so 59 trials are needed; 58 are insufficient. The rule-of-three approximation instead treats the upper failure probability as approximately 3/n, yielding n = 60 to make the failure rate at most 5%. If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is intended, α/2 is used for the lower bound, requiring 73 zero-failure trials. Thus, the one-sided exact-binomial answer is 59, while the conservative rule-of-three approximation gives 60.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that Clopper–Pearson limits are obtained by inverting exact binomial tail probabilities, using α/2 for a two-sided 100(1−α)% interval. For the requested zero-failure case, observe x=n successes in n trials. The exact one-sided 95% lower confidence bound is p_L = 0.05^(1/n). Requiring p_L ≥ 0.95 gives 0.05^(1/n) ≥ 0.95, or n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.95) = 58.40, so 59 trials are required. This is the exact one-sided binomial result. The familiar rule of three approximates the requirement as 3/n ≤ 0.05, yielding 60 trials. If “95% confidence” means a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval, use α/2 = 0.025 for the lower endpoint: p_L = 0.025^(1/n). Then n ≥ ln(0.025)/ln(0.95) = 71.36, so 72 trials with zero failures are required. Thus, 59 is the exact one-sided answer; 72 is the conservative two-sided Clopper–Pearson answer.
contexts.question: What is the exact calculation for the number of trials needed to demonstrate at least 95% success rate with 95% confidence, using the Clopper-Pearson or exact binomial test? Rule of three for zero failures.

contexts.context: ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluates manipulation policies on a managed fleet of low-cost SO-101 cells, supporting both single-arm and bimanual configurations. Each cell has one or two 5-DoF follower arms, three cameras, a Raspberry Pi 5 edge device, and a fixed workspace; object positions are randomized between rollouts. Policies run in isolated containers under a shared protocol, with one workstation handling inference and real-time control and a cloud backend scheduling jobs and streaming logs and video for monitoring. The benchmark covers 12 tasks and compares 7 policies. Every policy is trained or fine-tuned using 50 demonstrations per task. It contains 2,518 policy rollouts plus 600 reference demonstrations, for 3,118 total core episodes. Since 2,518 divided across 12 tasks and 7 policy-task combinations is approximately 30, the excerpt suggests about 30 evaluation rollouts per task per policy, although it does not explicitly state this allocation. Rollouts are scored by operators using three labels: successful, suboptimal, or failure; demonstrations are successful by construction. The excerpt does not identify the seven policies by name or provide the detailed task-specific success criteria.

contexts.context: ArmnetBench v0.1 evaluates manipulation policies on SO-101 follower-arm cells, using two single-arm cells and one bimanual cell in the reported deployment. The benchmark contains 12 tabletop tasks—8 single-arm and 4 bimanual—covering stacking, insertion, deformable objects, pick-and-place, and articulated-object manipulation. Each task-policy combination is evaluated for 30 rollouts, with two episodes removed because of incorrect manual resets, leaving those particular pairs with 29. Before every rollout, an operator resets the scene and randomizes object placement within a task-specific range; initial states are sampled independently rather than matched across policies. Each policy is trained or fine-tuned for the task using the same 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations. Rollouts use three synchronized camera views at 20 fps, and the operator assigns one of three labels: successful when the task goal is achieved cleanly, suboptimal when achieved with a poor-quality finish, or failure when the goal is not achieved. Seven policies are compared: ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, and MolmoAct 2.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

Reliability statistics: How should success rates, failures and mean cycles between interventions be reported for repeated robot tasks so they can be compared? Cover confidence intervals (Wilson, Clopper-Pearson), the number of trials needed to claim, for example, 95% success with 95% confidence, and how lab automation papers actually report these numbers.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Reliability Statistics for Robot Manipulation: Reporting Success Rates, Confidence Intervals, and Mean Cycles Between Interventions

## 1. The Problem: How the Field Currently Reports Success

The dominant metric in physical robot-manipulation evaluation is "success rate"—the percentage of autonomous runs that succeed. Kress-Gazit et al. (2024, preprint) argue that this practice is insufficient: "it is common for papers to report this number with little to no information regarding the number of runs, the initial conditions, and the success criteria, little to no narrative description of the behaviors and failures observed, and little to no statistical analysis of the findings" (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3). A recent audit of the five most-cited manipulation benchmarks (LIBERO, CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0) found that the majority of reported performance gaps between policies are statistically inconclusive when examined with paired Wald tests: across LIBERO, only 20.8% of 789 comparisons were provably significant at the 5% level (jiang2026whatarewe pages 5-7).

The following table summarizes how major benchmarks actually report results, their trial counts, and whether they include any form of uncertainty estimate.

*Table: Comparison of trial counts, success definitions, and uncertainty-reporting practices in major physical robot-manipulation studies. It highlights the historically common use of small raw success fractions and the more recent adoption of Wilson or other finite-sample confidence intervals.*

## 2. Binomial Confidence Intervals for Binary Task Success

### 2.1 Framing the Problem

Each manipulation trial is naturally modeled as a Bernoulli random variable X ∈ {0,1} with unknown success probability p (hietanen2021benchmarkingposeestimation pages 5-8). The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol defines reliability as "the probability of successfully completing a task or sub-task," computed from "a confidence level (CL), the number of successes (m), and the number of independent trials (n)" using the binomial cumulative distribution function (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9). This requires independent, identically distributed trials—a condition that Vincent et al. (2024, IEEE RA-L) emphasize must be ensured by a pre-specified testing plan, warning that practices such as "running policy rollouts until enough favorable outcomes are observed" violate the i.i.d. assumption (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4).

### 2.2 Clopper–Pearson (Exact) Intervals

The Clopper–Pearson method inverts exact binomial tail probabilities to produce a confidence interval whose coverage is guaranteed to be at least 1−α for all values of p (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 3-4, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 1-3). The two-sided 100(1−α)% interval allocates α/2 to each tail. Orawo (2021, Open Journal of Statistics) characterizes Clopper–Pearson as "very conservative" because its actual coverage typically exceeds the nominal level, especially at small sample sizes; mean coverage at n=15 with nominal 95% was measured at 0.974 (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 8-11). Vincent et al. (2024) note that the Clopper–Pearson lower bound is obtained from their uniformly most accurate (UMA) framework by "setting U = 0 in the test statistic," confirming it as a special case of the optimal bound and showing that their randomized UMA bound is always tighter (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5).

### 2.3 Wilson Score Intervals

Wilson score intervals provide better-behaved coverage than the normal-approximation (Wald) interval, particularly when p is near 0 or 1 or when sample sizes are small (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark (Vagas et al. 2026, IEEE RA-L) explicitly states that "we report Wilson score confidence intervals, which offer [well-behaved coverage] when sample sizes are small or observed proportions are close to 0 or 1" (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). Wilson intervals are increasingly adopted in 2025–2026 manipulation papers: Zhang et al. (2025, preprint) report "Wilson-score 95% confidence intervals for SR [success rate]" on their Mobile ALOHA VLA benchmarking (zhang2511experiencesfrombenchmarking pages 4-5); SafeVLA-Bench uses "Wilson score 95% intervals for binomial proportions"; and LADDER reports "95% Wilson confidence intervals over episodes."

Orawo (2021) recommends Wilson and likelihood intervals over both Wald and Clopper–Pearson for practical use, because they achieve near-nominal coverage without the excessive conservatism of the exact method (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 8-11).

### 2.4 Bayesian Approach

Kress-Gazit et al. (2024) illustrate a Bayesian alternative: model success as a Bernoulli distribution with unknown probability, place a uniform prior, and inspect the posterior distribution. They demonstrate that two policies achieving 13/20 (65%) and 14/20 (70%) have substantially overlapping posteriors, yielding only a 0.11 probability that the inferior policy is truly better—emphasizing that identical percentages from small samples cannot support superiority claims (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 9-13).

## 3. Minimum Number of Trials for Reliability Claims

The central sample-size question for robot reliability is: if all n trials succeed, how large must n be to claim that p ≥ p₀ with confidence 1−α? The exact one-sided binomial answer is n ≥ ⌈ln(α)/ln(p₀)⌉ (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6). For the canonical claim of "at least 95% success with 95% confidence," this yields n = ⌈ln(0.05)/ln(0.95)⌉ = ⌈58.40⌉ = 59 trials with zero failures. The well-known "rule of three" approximates this as 3/(1−p₀) = 60 (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6). If a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval is required instead, the lower tail uses α/2 = 0.025, yielding n = ⌈ln(0.025)/ln(0.95)⌉ = 72 (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6).

The following table provides the exact trial counts for several practically relevant reliability targets.

| Desired lower bound on success probability | Confidence level | Bound type | Required trials—all must succeed | Derivation / formula |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **59** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil58.40\rceil=59\) (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | 95% | Two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson | **72** | Equal tails use \(\alpha/2=0.025\): \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.025)/\ln(0.95)\right\rceil=\lceil71.92\rceil=72\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6) |
| \(p \ge 0.95\) | Approximately 95% | Rule-of-three approximation | **≈60** | \(n\approx3/(1-0.95)=60\); use the exact one-sided result, 59, for a formal claim (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6) |
| \(p \ge 0.90\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **29** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.90)\right\rceil=\lceil28.43\rceil=29\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5) |
| \(p \ge 0.99\) | 95% | One-sided exact binomial / Clopper–Pearson | **299** | \(n=\left\lceil\ln(0.05)/\ln(0.99)\right\rceil=\lceil298.07\rceil=299\) (meggendorfer2024whatarethe pages 27-31, vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5) |

*Table: Minimum all-success trial counts needed for selected lower-bound reliability claims. The distinction between a one-sided certification bound and a two-sided confidence interval materially changes the required sample size.*

**Critical implication for low-cost arms:** Most published manipulation papers use far fewer trials than the 59 required for a one-sided 95%/95% claim. ALOHA uses 25 real-robot trials per task (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 8-10); Mobile ALOHA uses 20 (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8); FurnitureBench uses 10 (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 6-7, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10); YCB protocols use 10 (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulation pages 34-35, calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35); and ArmnetBench uses 30 (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7). With 25 all-success trials, the one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson lower bound on p is only 0.05^(1/25) ≈ 0.887, not 0.95. To genuinely certify 95% success at 95% confidence, 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are necessary.

## 4. Mean Cycles Between Interventions and MTBF

### 4.1 In Lab Automation

Laboratory automation systems report reliability using mean time between failures (MTBF) measured in calendar days or operating hours. Croxatto et al. (2016, Clinical Microbiology and Infection, peer-reviewed) report that BD Kiestra TLA and WCA automated bacteriology systems achieve approximately 100 days MTBF, while the Copan WASPLab achieves approximately 95 days, with the caveat that "MTBF is difficult to specify because it depends substantially on system configuration, overall system complexity, the number and variety of samples processed each day, and user-induced factors" (croxatto2016laboratoryautomationin pages 11-13). In industrial manufacturing with Digital Twin/IIoT-enabled predictive maintenance, Mostofa (2024) reports baseline MTBF of 1,486.3 hours (SD 412.7; 95% CI [1,431.5, 1,541.1]) across 220 assets including robotic systems, improving to 2,176.8 hours post-intervention (mostofa2024digitaltwinand pages 26-27, mostofa2024digitaltwinand pages 27-29).

### 4.2 In Field Robotics

Honig and Oron-Gilad (2018, Frontiers in Psychology, peer-reviewed) note that "the Mean Time Between Failure (MTBF) for robots in field environments is often within a few hours" (honig2018understandingandresolving pages 3-5), highlighting the substantial gap between industrial automation and research robot reliability.

### 4.3 Explicit Gap: No Standard for Mean Cycles Between Interventions in Manipulation

**No published standard exists for reporting "mean cycles between interventions" (MCBI) as a reliability metric for robot manipulation tasks.** The NIST Assembly Task Board protocol uses binomial success probability and completion time (mean, SD, and 95% CI), but does not define a cycles-between-interventions metric (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9). Lab automation papers report MTBF in time units rather than task cycles (croxatto2016laboratoryautomationin pages 11-13). For teams running repeated pick-and-place or assembly cycles on low-cost arms, defining and reporting MCBI—the mean number of autonomous task cycles completed before a human must intervene to reset, fix a jam, or correct an error—would fill a genuine gap in the literature. This metric can be modeled as a geometric or negative-binomial random variable and reported with appropriate confidence intervals.

## 5. Best Practices for Reporting: A Synthesis

Based on the surveyed literature, the following reporting practices are recommended for teams benchmarking low-cost arms:

**What to report for each task:**
1. **Raw counts:** Report k successes out of n trials, not just percentages (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3).
2. **Confidence interval:** Report a Wilson score 95% CI for each success proportion (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3, zhang2511experiencesfrombenchmarking pages 4-5), or a Clopper–Pearson interval if conservative coverage is preferred (orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 4-6, orawo2021confidenceintervalsfor pages 3-4). If using Bayesian methods, show posterior distributions (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9).
3. **Success criterion:** Define success semantically and unambiguously. The Cross-Embodiment Gripper Benchmark defines success as "lifting the object at least 5 cm within 3 seconds and holding it for 3 seconds without slipping, with a 10-second timeout" (vagas2026acrossembodimentgripper pages 2-3). FurnitureBench uses phase-completion scores alongside binary success (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 8-10). ArmnetBench uses three-way grading: successful, suboptimal, or failure (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).
4. **Initial conditions:** Specify the randomization range, whether initial conditions are matched across policies, and whether evaluations are interleaved (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 3-5).
5. **Failure modes:** Describe observed failure modes qualitatively (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 1-3).
6. **Completion time:** Report mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for task-completion time (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9).
7. **Trial independence:** Verify and state that trials are independent—no cherry-picking, no stopping-when-good, no environmental drift (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 3-4).

**How many trials to run:**
- For a **screening evaluation** during development: 20–30 trials per task are standard practice (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9) and will give Wilson 95% CI half-widths of roughly ±15–20 percentage points at 80% success.
- For a **formal reliability claim** of p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence: 59 consecutive successes with zero failures are required (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6).
- For **comparing two policies:** Use at least 20 trials per policy under matched initial conditions and apply a paired test or Bayesian comparison (kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 7-9, kressgazit2024robotlearningas pages 9-13). Jiang et al. (2026, preprint) show that even with hundreds of comparisons, reported performance gaps are often statistically inconclusive (jiang2026whatarewe pages 5-7).

## 6. Placing Low-Cost Arms in the Published Literature

### 6.1 Available Benchmarks for SO-101 and ALOHA-Class Arms

**ArmnetBench v0.1** (Selvaraj et al. 2026, preprint) is the most directly relevant benchmark for SO-101 arms. It evaluates 7 policies (ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct 2) across 12 tasks on a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, using 30 rollouts per task-policy pair with 50 demonstrations and three-way operator scoring (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3).

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al. 2026, ICLR, peer-reviewed) provides the open-source software stack supporting SO-100, SO-101, Koch-v1.1, and ALOHA hardware. It integrates LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks and standardized dataset formats, but the paper itself does not report real-world success-rate benchmarks with confidence intervals for specific arms (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 10-11).

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al. 2024, preprint) provides a multi-embodiment dataset spanning Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, AgileX dual-arm robot, and a humanoid, with 107k demonstrations across 479 tasks, enabling cross-embodiment comparison.

### 6.2 Explicit Gaps

- **No published peer-reviewed paper benchmarks the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm** on any standard manipulation protocol with reported confidence intervals. Any reliability claim for PiPER would need to be generated de novo.
- **No published paper provides a head-to-head reliability comparison** (with binomial confidence intervals or MTBF) between low-cost arms (SO-101, PiPER, ALOHA) and industrial arms (UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) on matched tasks. RoboMIND includes multiple embodiments but reports imitation-learning success rates rather than hardware-reliability metrics.
- **ABB YuMi** and **Kinova** arms appear in the manipulation literature but not in published benchmarks with the statistical rigor described here.

### 6.3 Repeatable Protocol Recommendation

For teams with PiPER and SO-101 arms seeking to generate publishable, comparable data:

1. **Select a standard object set** (YCB objects are freely available with 3D models) (calli2015benchmarkinginmanipulationa pages 34-35).
2. **Use the NIST Assembly Task Board protocol** for assembly tasks: record start/finish times, autonomous operation only (no manual intervention permitted), and report binomial reliability bounds (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9).
3. **For imitation-learning policies**, follow the ArmnetBench protocol: 50 demonstrations, 30+ rollouts per task-policy pair, three-way scoring, randomized initial placement (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).
4. **Report Wilson score 95% CIs** for all success proportions, state the one-sided or two-sided convention, and report raw k/n alongside percentages.
5. **For reliability certification**, run at least 59 consecutive successful trials per task to claim p ≥ 0.95 at 95% confidence (vincent2024howgeneralizableis pages 4-5, budde2025soundstatisticalmodel pages 3-6).
6. **For comparing with Franka or UR5e results**, use matched tasks from FMB (25 trials, Franka), FurnitureBench (10 trials, Franka Panda), or RoboMIND protocols and recompute confidence intervals on the published raw counts.

info.query:
We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

Reliability statistics: How should success rates, failures and mean cycles between interventions be reported for repeated robot tasks so they can be compared? Cover confidence intervals (Wilson, Clopper-Pearson), the number of trials needed to claim, for example, 95% success with 95% confidence, and how lab automation papers actually report these numbers.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
